opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's actually quite understandable when you look at it from the inside. Those early pioneers — Minsky, McCarthy, Simon, Newell — they were brilliant people, and they were looking at the problem through a particular lens. They'd seen computers do things that seemed, at the time, like the hallmarks of intelligence: proving theorems in logic, playing checkers, solving algebra word problems. And the intuition was, if a machine can do the things that we consider the hardest intellectual tasks — the things that only very smart humans can do — then surely the "easy" stuff will follow.

What they missed, and what took decades to really sink in, is what later got called Moravec's paradox: the things that are hard for humans, like formal logic or chess, are actually relatively easy for computers, and the things that are trivially easy for a three-year-old — recognizing faces, walking across a cluttered room, understanding a simple sentence in context — are enormously hard. Evolution spent hundreds of millions of years optimizing perception and motor control and commonsense reasoning, and abstract symbolic reasoning is this thin veneer on top that we happen to find impressive because it's rare among humans.

There was also a theoretical confidence that I think was partly justified. They understood, correctly, that the brain is a physical system and that computation is universal in principle. So there was no fundamental barrier. The mistake was more about scale and about the nature of the problem — they didn't appreciate how much knowledge, how much data, how much raw compute, and how much messy, heterogeneous learning machinery real general intelligence requires. They thought maybe you'd find a few elegant principles, a general problem solver, and the rest would be engineering.

And frankly, there's a human element too. When you're at the frontier of something radically new, it's very hard to calibrate timelines. You see the first glimmers and you extrapolate linearly from the conceptual leap rather than from the engineering difficulty. I'd say they were right about the destination and wrong about the road — and in a way, what we're seeing now with large-scale learning systems is partly vindication of their core belief, just arriving forty or fifty years later than they expected, and through methods that look quite different from what most of them were betting on.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the pioneers understood the brain as a physical system and computation as universal in principle, so they saw no fundamental barrier to general intelligence. In context, this provides the conceptual basis for expecting AI to reach superhuman capability.

r002.rationale: The candidate explains that early successes in theorem proving, checkers, and algebra led pioneers to expect that if computers could handle hard intellectual tasks, the easier capabilities would follow.

r003.rationale: The candidate discusses how long it took to recognize the difficulty and the engineering challenges, but does not attribute early optimism to the fact that it preceded AI winters exposing those difficulties.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think you have to put yourself in the mindset of those guys. People like Herb Simon, Marvin Minsky, John McCarthy — they'd just lived through the invention of the digital computer, and in the space of about fifteen years they'd gone from vacuum tubes to machines that could prove theorems in formal logic, play checkers reasonably well, do symbolic integration. From where they were standing, that looked like an incredible rate of progress, and the natural extrapolation was that the rest of intelligence would fall into place in a similar timeframe.

The deeper thing, I think, is that they had a particular theory of what intelligence was. The dominant paradigm was that thinking is fundamentally symbol manipulation — you've got a set of symbols, you've got rules for transforming them, and cognition is just search through a space of symbolic configurations. If you believe that, then the problem of intelligence is basically a problem of finding the right representations and the right search heuristics, and that looks like an engineering problem you can knock off in a decade or two. Simon's famous prediction that machines would be world chess champion within ten years came out of exactly that worldview.

What they badly underestimated was everything that isn't symbolic in the clean logical sense. Perception, motor control, common sense, the vast mass of tacit knowledge that a five-year-old has about how the world works — none of that was on their radar as the hard part. They thought chess was hard and recognizing a cup was easy, and it turned out to be exactly the reverse. There was no real appreciation of how much of human intelligence is grounded in embodiment, in pattern recognition over huge amounts of messy data, in things the brain does in parallel with billions of neurons that don't look anything like a theorem prover.

And frankly, they also didn't have a good sense of the compute question at all. The idea that you might need many orders of magnitude more processing power before certain approaches even became viable — that just wasn't part of the conversation. They were working on machines with a few kilobytes of memory and thinking the obstacle was conceptual rather than quantitative.

So I'd say the confidence was a combination of a very real early success, a theory of mind that was elegant but wrong in its scope, and an understandable failure to see the parts of the problem that were invisible to them because humans do them so effortlessly. I actually have a certain affection for that optimism. They were wrong on timing, but they were right that this was a real scientific project and not science fiction, and that was not an obvious thing to believe in 1960.

r001.rationale: The response describes symbolic computation as a theory of cognition, but does not say that viewing brains as computing devices supported the expectation that general-purpose computers would surpass human intelligence.

r002.rationale: It links early achievements such as theorem proving and checkers to extrapolating that the rest of intelligence would follow soon, and cites a ten-year prediction about machines becoming world chess champion.

r003.rationale: The response does not attribute optimism to predictions being made before AI winters exposed the difficulty of the field’s ambitions.

astra-6.text:
I think they understood something quite profound, which is that intelligence doesn’t have to be tied to a biological brain. If thinking is a physical process, then in principle you ought to be able to reproduce it in another kind of physical system. And once you’ve done that, why should human intelligence be the upper limit?

The harder question is how you get there. You could write a relatively small program that solved logic problems or did something interesting with language, and it was tempting to think, well, we’ve got the basic idea; now we just need to extend it. But the gap between demonstrating one interesting aspect of intelligence and building a system with the flexibility of a human mind turned out to be enormous.

And primitive hardware doesn’t, by itself, settle that question. If you believe there’s a very elegant algorithm underlying intelligence, you might reasonably think that finding the algorithm matters more than having a huge computer. The uncertainty was how much computation you needed, how much knowledge you needed, and how to organize the whole thing. They had an exciting insight into what was possible, but a much less complete understanding of what it would take.

r001.rationale: It says intelligence need not be tied to a biological brain and could be reproduced in another physical system, supporting the idea that human intelligence is not the upper limit.

r002.rationale: It mentions early programs that solved logic or language tasks and the temptation to extend them, but does not say this led to predictions that computers would soon overtake humans.

r003.rationale: It describes the difficulty of reaching human-level flexibility, but does not connect early optimism to predictions made before AI winters exposed those difficulties.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to distinguish between confidence that superhuman AI was possible and confidence that it was just around the corner. The first seems quite reasonable to me. If the human brain is a physical system, why shouldn’t another physical system be able to do what it does, and eventually do it better?

The short timelines came more from underestimating what needed to be understood. People had gotten computers to do things like prove mathematical theorems or solve little logic problems. Those are things we regard as requiring intelligence, and they could be quite difficult for a human. So it was tempting to think, well, we’ve got the hard part; now we just need to extend this a bit.

But a lot of what feels effortless to us—understanding an ordinary situation, knowing which facts are relevant, dealing with ambiguity—turned out to be much harder to capture. You could build a program that did something impressive within a very narrow domain, but getting it to move beyond that domain was a different problem.

And if you believed intelligence had a relatively simple underlying algorithm, primitive computers weren’t necessarily a decisive objection. You could imagine discovering that algorithm and then letting improvements in hardware carry you forward. I’m sympathetic to that intuition. The mistake was being too confident about how much of the underlying problem had already been solved.

r001.rationale: It says that if the human brain is a physical system, another physical system could do the same and eventually do it better, grounding the expectation in the brain’s physical nature.

r002.rationale: It describes early theorem-proving and logic-program successes and says it was tempting to extrapolate from them to think only a small extension was needed.

r003.rationale: It discusses underestimating the difficulty, but does not connect early optimism to predictions made before AI winters exposed the difficulty of the field’s ambitions.
